Problem: Algorithms - 19
P3
Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a unique minimum spanning
P4
tree if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied: (1) For every partition
P5
of the vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight connecting the two
P6
subsets is unique. (2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight
P7
is unique.
P8
Solution:
**Proof:** Let G = (V, E) be a connected weighted graph. We will show that
G has a unique minimum spanning tree if and only if it satisfies both properties (1) and (2).
We denote by MST(G) any minimum spanning tree of G (if one exists), and by w(e) the
weight of an edge e ∈E.
**(⇒)** *If G has a unique MST, then properties (1) and (2) hold.*
Suppose T is the *unique* minimum spanning tree of G. We show that T’s uniqueness
forces (1) and (2).
- **Property (1):** Consider an arbitrary partition (cut) of V into two disjoint subsets
X and Y = V \ X. Let emin be an edge of minimum weight connecting X to Y (i.e. one
endpoint in X and one in Y ).
We claim emin is unique.
If not, suppose there are two
distinct edges e1, e2 crossing the cut [X, Y ] each of minimum weight. By the cut property
of MSTs, a minimum spanning tree must contain at least one minimum-weight edge across
every cut. Without loss of generality, assume e1 ∈T. Now form a new
spanning tree T ′ by removing e1 from T and adding the other edge e2.
Because e1 and e2 have the same weight w(e1) = w(e2), the total weight w(T ′) = w(T) −
w(e1) + w(e2) = w(T). Thus T ′ is also a minimum spanning tree of G. Moreover, T ′ ̸= T
(since e2 /∈T and e1 /∈T ′), contradicting the uniqueness of T. Therefore no such pair e1, e2
can exist, and *every* cut [X, Y ] has a unique minimum-weight crossing edge. This proves
- **Property (2):** Now consider any simple cycle C in G. Let emax be the edge of C
with maximum weight. We claim emax is unique on C. If not, suppose two different edges
f1, f2 ∈C share the maximum weight on C (so w(f1) = w(f2) is the largest on the cycle).
Because T is a spanning tree, it cannot contain all edges of C (as that would form a cycle
within T). At least one of f1 or f2 is absent from T. Without loss of generality, assume
f1 /∈T. Now consider *adding* f1 to T. This introduces a unique cycle C′ in T ∪{f1} (since
a spanning tree plus one edge yields exactly one cycle). The cycle C′ is a subgraph of G
that includes the newly added edge f1 and some path in T that connects the endpoints of
f1. Observe that C′ must contain the other edge f2 as well, because f2 lies on the unique
cycle C connecting the same endpoints in G (and T spans all vertices). Thus C′ contains
both f1 and f2. In C′, these two edges tie for the largest weight (since w(f1) = w(f2) and
no edge on C′ can be heavier than f1, f2 by construction).
Now construct a new spanning tree T ′′ by **removing** f2 from T ∪{f1} (breaking the
cycle C′). The resulting T ′′ is a spanning tree because removing one edge from a cycle in
a connected graph leaves it connected. Moreover, w(T ′′) = w(T) + w(f1) −w(f2) = w(T)
since w(f1) = w(f2). So T ′′ is another minimum spanning tree of G, different from T (it
contains f1 but not f2, whereas T contains f2 but not f1). This contradicts the uniqueness of
T. Therefore no cycle in G can have two edges tying for maximum weight. In other words,
emax on any cycle is unique, establishing (2).
**(⇐)** *If properties (1) and (2) hold for G, then G has a unique minimum spanning
tree.*
Assume now that every cut of G has a unique lightest edge, and every cycle of G has
a unique heaviest edge. We must show that under these conditions, there is **only one**
minimum spanning tree.
Suppose (for sake of contradiction) that G has two different minimum spanning trees, say
T1 and T2, with w(T1) = w(T2) minimal. Consider the symmetric difference T1△T2, which
decomposes into a collection of simple cycles. (Any edge e ∈T1△T2 lies in exactly one of T1
or T2, and following alternately edges from T1 and T2 from such an e will eventually close a
cycle since T1 and T2 are both spanning trees.)
Let C be one such cycle in T1△T2, and let e∗be the edge on C of maximum weight. By
property (2), e∗is unique on C. There are two cases to consider:
- **Case 1:** e∗∈T1 (so e∗/∈T2). Then e∗is the unique heaviest edge of cycle C.
Because e∗/∈T2, the cycle C in T1△T2 must contain another edge f ∈T2 (and not in T1)
that connects the same two components formed by removing e∗from T1. (Equivalently, if we
remove e∗from T1, we partition V into two parts; since T2 is spanning, it must have some
edge f crossing this cut.) By property (1), e∗is the unique minimum-weight edge crossing
that cut, so in particular w(e∗) < w(f). But f lies on the same cycle C, so f must have
weight *less* than e∗(since e∗is the unique largest on C). This is a contradiction: we cannot
have simultaneously w(f) > w(e∗) and w(f) < w(e∗).
- **Case 2:** e∗∈T2 (so e∗/∈T1). This situation is symmetric to Case 1. Removing e∗
from T2 partitions V into two parts; some edge g ∈T1 crosses that cut. By property (1), e∗
is the unique lightest crossing, so w(e∗) < w(g). Yet e∗was the unique heaviest on cycle C,
forcing w(e∗) > w(g) since g ∈C as well. Again we have a contradiction.
In each case we derived an impossibility from the assumption T1 ̸= T2. Therefore, no two
distinct minimum spanning trees can exist under properties (1) and (2). In other words, the
MST of G is **unique**.
Combining both directions, we conclude that G has a unique minimum spanning tree if
and only if **(1)** every cut of G has a unique minimum-weight crossing edge, and **(2)**
every cycle of G has a unique maximum-weight edge. This completes the proof.
